subject: Creativity
title: MVP: The Minimum Viable Product Philosophy
description: A 60-second lesson on MVP: The Minimum Viable Product Philosophy.

hook.text: Dropbox's MVP was a 3-minute video showing a product that didn't exist yet. 75,000 people signed up overnight.

buildup.text: Eric Ries defined MVP as the simplest version of a product that can test whether customers actually want it — before.

discovery.text: The purpose isn't to launch something incomplete. It's to maximize learning with minimum effort — validated learning.

twist.text: Zappos' MVP was simpler: the founder photographed shoes at local stores and listed them online.

climax.text: Companies that validate with MVPs are 3x more likely to succeed than those that build full products before testing.

punchline.text: Build the smallest thing that answers the biggest question.

quiz.question: What was Dropbox's MVP?
options: A 3-minute demo video of a product that didn't exist

details.summary: The minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that can be released to test a core hypothesis with real users. The MVP philosophy prioritizes learning over perfection, getting feedback before investing in features that users may not want.
details.whyItMatters: MVP thinking prevents the common mistake of spending months building something nobody wants. It shifts development from assumption-driven to evidence-driven, saving enormous resources.
takeaways: An MVP tests a core hypothesis with minimal investment
Learning from real users is more valuable than perfecting features
Successful products like Dropbox launched as simple MVPs

faq.question: How minimal should an MVP be?
faq.answer: Minimal enough to test the core assumption but complete enough to provide a genuine experience. An MVP is not a broken product; it is a focused one. It should do one thing well enough to learn whether users want it.

faq.question: Is MVP release not risky for brand reputation?
faq.answer: If the MVP is too rough, it can damage perception. The key is to be transparent about what users are testing. Early adopters typically accept roughness in exchange for early access and influence over the product's direction.
